planting.note: Set out potted divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich soil so roots establish before summer heat arrives.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, organically rich soil in dappled shade, where a few hours of morning sun will deepen the bronze-black foliage color without scorching it. Mulch generously to keep roots cool and moist through summer, since this cultivar sulks in dry spells. Fragrant, pink-tinged white bottlebrush spikes appear on dark purple stems in late summer into fall, rising well above the compact foliage mound. Divide congested clumps in early spring only when needed, as plants resent frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Transplant nursery divisions in spring into moist, fertile shade beds and keep evenly watered while roots settle in.

directions: Give this cultivar rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, where its finely cut chocolate-purple foliage colors best and its black stems stay upright. Arching wands of raspberry-pink buds open to pale, heavily fragrant flowers in late summer and fall, making it a strong late-season pollinator draw. Avoid hot afternoon sun and drought, both of which scorch the dark foliage and shorten bloom. Top-dress annually with compost rather than dividing often, since established clumps flower best left undisturbed for several years.

planting.note: Site divisions in spring at the back of a shaded border, allowing room for stems that reach well over head height by autumn.

directions: This is the largest common bugbane cultivar, so give it deep, cool, humus-rich soil in part shade and stake it against wind if the site is exposed. Long, branching bottlebrush racemes of sweetly scented white flowers open in early autumn atop coarsely toothed green foliage, towering over most shade perennials. Keep soil consistently moist through summer since dry conditions stunt growth and reduce flowering. Because of its imposing size, use it as a dramatic woodland-edge specimen rather than in small borders.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded border or streamside planting.

directions: Choose this compact, threadleaf-foliaged goatsbeard for smaller shade gardens where the full-size species would overwhelm the space. The deeply cut, almost Japanese-maple-like leaves form a graceful mound topped by creamy plumes in early to midsummer, though flowering is lighter than the species. Keep soil evenly moist, especially in warmer zones, since foliage browns quickly in drought. Mass several plants along a pond edge or woodland path for the best textural effect.

planting.note: Set divisions out in spring into rich, moisture-retentive soil, choosing part shade in warmer climates and more sun where water is reliable.

directions: This mid-sized hybrid between the giant and dwarf goatsbeards bridges the gap between the two parent species, with bronze-toned stems carrying narrow, horizontal astilbe-like plumes of creamy flowers in early summer. It tolerates heat and humidity better than most Aruncus selections, performing reliably through Zone 7b summers. Provide organically rich, consistently moist soil and part shade in the South, or full sun further north if irrigation is dependable. Fall color turns the fern-like foliage attractive shades of red before dieback.

common_name: Misty Lace Goatsbeard (Compact Astilbe-Like Goat's Beard)

planting.note: Install divisions in spring into rich, evenly moist soil; this heat-tolerant selection also suits warmer southern gardens.

directions: A patented compact hybrid selected for wide, mounding growth of finely dissected, astilbe-like foliage on dark red stems, this cultivar suits both cold northern gardens and hot, humid southern ones. Airy plumes of tiny white flowers rise above the foliage mound in late spring, forming an attractive groundcover-like drift when massed. Grow in fertile, organically rich soil that stays consistently moist, siting it in part shade where summers run hot and in fuller sun where irrigation is reliable. Established clumps need little maintenance beyond an annual spring cleanup of old foliage.

common_name: Key West Astilbe (Red-Emerging Reblooming False Spirea)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded bed for the longest bloom window.

directions: Bred from a cross of 'Sprite' and 'Fanal', this compact simplicifolia-type astilbe emerges with red-tinted new growth that matures to bronze-green foliage edged in red. Red flower buds fade to soft pink over an unusually long six-week bloom period from midsummer into early fall, and plants often rebloom later in the season. Keep the soil consistently moist, since astilbes wilt quickly in dry conditions, and mulch to conserve moisture in shaded beds. Its compact size makes it well suited to container culture or the front of a woodland border.

common_name: Bressingham Beauty Astilbe (Salmon-Pink Arendsii False Spirea)

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring into rich, moisture-retentive soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

directions: A sport of the older 'Cattleya' cultivar, this Arendsii astilbe produces long, gracefully arching plumes of dusty salmon-rose flowers over burgundy-tinged spring foliage that matures to dark green. Provide evenly moist, organically rich soil and part shade with a few hours of filtered morning sun for the best flower color and stem strength. Established clumps make excellent cut flowers and naturalize well along stream banks or in the middle of a mixed shade border. Divide when flowering declines, usually every three to four years, to keep clumps vigorous.
